title: Cognitive biases
examples: What is the difference between a heuristic and a cognitive bias?
Can you give me an example of confirmation bias in the news?
Are heuristics always bad for thinking?

explain.say: Today we will explore how our minds take shortcuts. These shortcuts are called heuristics.

items: A mental shortcut for quick decisions
It helps us make fast judgments

explain.say: One type of heuristic is availability. We judge things by how easily we remember them. For example, we think plane crashes are very common because we see them on the news.

Next we look at confirmation bias. This is when we favor information that matches what we already believe. For instance, if you believe a certain diet is best, you will only read articles supporting it.

items: Action: Search for Diet X articles

explain.say: A real-life example involves buying a car. If you are convinced a certain brand is reliable, you will only notice positive reviews for that brand, ignoring negative ones.
The common mistake is thinking that because we feel strongly about something, it must be true. To avoid this, you must actively search for opposing viewpoints.

items: Do not stop reading after agreement

explain.say: If you are trying to decide on a new hobby, you might use the heuristic of representativeness. You might assume someone who loves hiking must like camping too. This is a mental guess.

faq.q: What is the difference between a heuristic and a bias?
faq.a: A heuristic is a mental shortcut used for quick thinking. A bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from norm or rationality in judgment. You might ask, 'Are they the same thing?' or 'How are they related?'
asks: What is the difference between a shortcut and a bias?

faq.q: Can I get an example of confirmation bias in history?
faq.a: Someone might only read historical accounts that confirm their existing view of a historical figure. They might ask, 'How does this apply to history?' or 'Is this bias in reading?'
asks: Give me a historical example of this bias.

faq.q: Are all mental shortcuts bad for thinking?
faq.a: No, heuristics are useful because they save us time and mental energy. However, they can lead to errors when the situation is complex. You could also ask, 'Are there good shortcuts?' or 'When are heuristics useful?'

faq.q: How do I avoid confirmation bias when I am arguing with someone?
faq.a: The best way is to force yourself to argue for the side you disagree with. You should also ask, 'What evidence contradicts my view?' or 'How can I argue the other side?'
asks: How to stop believing only what I want?
Tips for overcoming confirmation bias in debate.

faq.a: It is judging something based on how much it resembles a typical example. For example, assuming a quiet person must be a librarian. You might ask, 'What is pattern matching in thinking?' or 'Is this related to stereotypes?'
asks: Can I confuse representativeness with stereotypes?

facts: Heuristics are mental rules of thumb that help us make quick decisions.
Confirmation bias causes people to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information that confirms their existing beliefs.
The availability heuristic makes us overestimate the likelihood of events that are easily recalled.
These cognitive shortcuts are efficient but can lead to systematic errors in judgment.

quiz.say: A student only reads news articles that support their belief in climate change.
quiz.why: This is confirmation bias because the student is favoring information that matches their existing belief.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the student is not judging by how easily they recall information.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the student is not judging based on how typical the articles seem.
wrong.3: This is too general; confirmation bias names the specific pattern of error.

quiz.say: Judging that a person who loves nature must also enjoy camping.
quiz.why: This uses representativeness because the student is assuming similarity to a typical example.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the student is not relying on a recent, vivid memory.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the student is not filtering information to confirm a belief.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the student is not sticking too closely to the first piece of information given.

quiz.say: We think plane crashes are more common than they actually are because we see them on the news.
quiz.why: This is the availability heuristic because the vivid media coverage makes the memory easily available.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the error is based on recall ease, not just overestimating one's own knowledge.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the student is not filtering information to confirm a belief.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the student is not comparing the crash to a typical pattern.
